patient.name: Thomas Gu
patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral foot numbness and weakness for 14 months with recent right wrist drop
patient.hpi: Thomas Gu is a 49-year-old sales director presenting to neurology after developing progressive bilateral foot numbness over 14 months followed by recent onset right wrist drop noted upon awakening 3 weeks ago. He initially attributed his foot symptoms to long hours standing during business travel and tight footwear. His primary care physician obtained EMG 3 months ago which reportedly showed mild sensory neuropathy and attributed it to borderline prediabetes (HbA1c 5.9%). However, the acute onset of right wrist drop was alarming, and the patient was referred urgently. He reports left hand numbness as well (ring and little finger distribution). He has been evaluated for occupational exposures: he works in pharmaceutical sales and denies any chemical exposures. He has noted a 6 kg unintentional weight loss over the past year which he initially attributed to stress and dietary changes. He has also noted intermittent abdominal fullness and early satiety for 6 months. He is a non-smoker and drinks socially but not heavily. He has never used intravenous drugs. He has a maternal grandmother who had 'Charcot foot' from diabetes, and he was therefore not concerned initially. His right wrist drop is now impacting his ability to drive and write, prompting this urgent referral.
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: bilateral foot numbness, right wrist drop (acute, 3 weeks), left hand ring/little finger numbness, 6 kg unintentional weight loss, intermittent early satiety and abdominal fullness. Negative: fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, cough, edema, rash, joint pain, bowel blood.

family_history: Maternal grandmother: type 2 diabetes with diabetic foot complications ('Charcot foot'). Father: hypertension. No known hereditary neuropathy.

social_history.note: Senior pharmaceutical sales director. Frequent business travel. Married, one child. Non-smoker. Social alcohol (3-4 drinks per week on average). No illicit drugs. No occupational chemical exposures confirmed by occupational health review.

Neuropathy and Inflammatory Workup.value: Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia — no M-spike; gamma fraction 28% (elevated)

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL (H), MCV 76 fL (H), Platelets 484 K/uL (H), Eosinophils 980 cells/uL (H), Total Protein 8.8 g/dL (H), Albumin 3.2 g/dL (H), LDH 386 U/L (H), HbA1c 5.9 % (H), ESR 88 mm/hr (H), CRP 28.4 mg/L (H), ANCA (MPO/PR3) ANCA-MPO positive, titer 1:160  (H), SPEP Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia — no M-spike; gamma fraction 28% (elevated)  (H), Fecal occult blood POSITIVE  (H), Ferritin 4 ng/mL (H), Iron 28 ug/dL (H), TIBC 488 ug/dL (H).

report.summary: MONONEURITIS MULTIPLEX confirmed. Acute right radial neuropathy (wrist drop). Subacute left ulnar neuropathy. Background bilateral peroneal axonal neuropathy. Pattern NOT consistent with prediabetic neuropathy or diabetic polyneuropathy. Consistent with vasculitic neuropathy.

motor.flag: SEVERELY ABNORMAL — near-complete axonal loss right posterior interosseous nerve
reduced amplitude — left ulnar axonal loss

sensory.flag: SEVERELY REDUCED — axonal loss right radial sensory

emg.summary: MONONEURITIS MULTIPLEX — acute severe right radial mononeuropathy (4+ fibrillations), subacute left ulnar neuropathy, chronic bilateral peroneal neuropathy. Three separate nerve territories involved over time — classic vasculitic neuropathy pattern.

report.overall_impression: MONONEURITIS MULTIPLEX confirming vasculitic neuropathy. Three separate nerves in separate vascular territories: right radial (acute), left ulnar (subacute), bilateral peroneal (chronic). Temporal and anatomical dissociation rules out all single-diagnosis alternatives. URGENT: nerve biopsy and tissue confirmation for vasculitis. Systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis (MPA or EGPA given eosinophilia) is the primary diagnosis.

output.test_type: Sural Nerve + Peroneus Brevis Muscle Biopsy

report.summary: VASCULITIC NEUROPATHY CONFIRMED. Epineurial necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of medium-sized vessel wall. Transmural eosinophilic and neutrophilic infiltrate. Axonal degeneration in multiple fascicles. Eosinophilic infiltrate in vessel wall raises EGPA.
report.histology: Sural nerve: epineurial arteriole with transmural inflammation — eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes infiltrating vessel wall, fibrinoid necrosis, luminal occlusion. Multiple fascicles show severe axonal degeneration. Myelinated fiber density severely reduced. Eosinophil count in nerve: 28 per high-power field. Muscle biopsy: perivascular eosinophilic infiltrate, no granulomas. Congo red negative.
report.interpretation: EOSINOPHILIC VASCULITIC NEUROPATHY — histological features most consistent with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss) given prominent eosinophilic infiltration. EGPA: myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA positive in ~40% of EGPA cases. Eosinophilia + MPO-ANCA + eosinophilic vasculitis + mononeuritis multiplex = EGPA diagnosis.

report.summary: CT CHEST: Bilateral ground-glass opacities in both lower lobes consistent with eosinophilic lung disease (eosinophilic pneumonia pattern). Small bilateral pleural effusions. No nodules, no cavitation. CT ABDOMEN/PELVIS: Circumferential wall thickening of distal ileum and cecum — eosinophilic gastroenteritis pattern. Mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy. No mass lesion. GI wall thickening explains iron deficiency anemia (GI blood loss from eosinophilic gastroenteritis), thrombocytosis (reactive), and hypoalbuminemia.
report.clinical_significance: Multi-organ EGPA confirmed: lung (eosinophilic pneumonia) + GI (eosinophilic gastroenteritis) + peripheral nerve (vasculitic neuropathy). Classic EGPA triad: asthma/eosinophilic lung disease + peripheral eosinophilia + neuropathy.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: BAL Differential — Eosinophils 42% % (H), BAL Macrophages 38% % (H), BAL Neutrophils 18% % (H), BAL Lymphocytes 2% % (H).

report.summary: Echocardiogram: LVEF 60% (normal). Mildly increased pericardial effusion (8 mm, trivial-small). No wall motion abnormalities. No valvular abnormalities. No evidence of eosinophilic endocarditis. Pericardial effusion is likely EGPA-related (cardiac involvement in EGPA 20-50%).
report.clinical_significance: Cardiac EGPA involvement present (pericardial effusion). Serial cardiac monitoring indicated. Cardiac EGPA can cause myocarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy — require close cardiology follow-up during treatment. Pericardial effusion is currently trivial and does not require drainage.

report.summary: Colonoscopy: patchy erythema and mucosal edema from cecum through distal ileum. Biopsies show eosinophilic infiltrate (>50 eosinophils per high-power field) in ileum and cecum — consistent with eosinophilic gastroenteritis. No polyps. No malignancy. No IBD features.
report.interpretation: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis confirmed — explains iron deficiency anemia (mucosal blood loss), abdominal symptoms (early satiety, fullness), and reactive thrombocytosis. EGPA multi-organ confirmation: lung + nerve + GI + heart (pericardium). Treatment: systemic corticosteroids address all organ manifestations.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss) with mononeuritis multiplex
critical_actions: Recognize mononeuritis multiplex — do NOT attribute to prediabetes or prior NCS showing mild distal sensory neuropathy
Order ANCA (MPO/PR3) urgently in any patient with mononeuritis multiplex — vasculitic neuropathy
Multi-organ assessment: lung, heart, GI — EGPA is systemic
Nerve biopsy to confirm vasculitis histologically before committing to cyclophosphamide
Echocardiogram — cardiac EGPA can cause fatal myocarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute wrist drop to pressure palsy without workup — mononeuritis multiplex requires vasculitis exclusion
Do not attribute to prediabetes — HbA1c 5.9% prediabetes does not cause mononeuritis multiplex
Do not delay treatment while awaiting all biopsies in patient with rapidly progressing vasculitic neuropathy
Do not start IVIG — this is vasculitic neuropathy requiring steroids and immunosuppression, not CIDP

differential.key_distinguishing: HbA1c 5.9% in prediabetic range does not cause acute wrist drop; length-dependent bilateral symmetric pattern expected; mononeuritis multiplex is not diabetic neuropathy
MPO-ANCA present in both MPA and EGPA; EGPA is distinguished by eosinophilia >1000 cells/uL (at peak), eosinophilic organ involvement (lung, GI), nerve biopsy eosinophilic infiltrate

differential.condition: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
differential.key_distinguishing: HNPP causes painless focal pressure palsies at common compression sites; systemic features absent; ANCA negative; eosinophilia absent; family history negative
MMN causes conduction block without axonal loss; no sensory involvement; anti-GM1 IgM typically positive; no systemic features

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: Prior NCS labeled 'mild diabetic neuropathy' and HbA1c 5.9% prediabetes create strong anchoring bias
KEY ALERT: ACUTE WRIST DROP is never attributable to prediabetes — demands urgent vasculitis workup
EGPA triad: eosinophilic lung disease + peripheral eosinophilia + neuropathy — systemic features point beyond pure neuropathy
Unintentional weight loss + early satiety + GI symptoms + microcytic anemia = systemic disease, not isolated neuropathy
MPO-ANCA is positive in ~40% of EGPA (unlike PR3-ANCA which is rarer) — must be tested
Eosinophilia in peripheral blood + eosinophilic vasculitis on nerve biopsy = EGPA vs MPA (eosinophilia distinguishes EGPA)
Mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) is FDA-approved for relapsing/refractory EGPA — modern alternative to cyclophosphamide
